Antônio Francisco Lisboa, called Aleijadinho ("little cripple"), was a sculptor, carver and architect of colonial Brazil, the great master of Brazilian baroque. He was born in Vila Rica, now Ouro Preto, in 1730 or 1738, the son of a Portuguese builder and an enslaved African woman.

He worked in the towns of Minas Gerais that the gold rush had made rich. Lay brotherhoods there paid for fine churches. His best known works:

  • the church of São Francisco de Assis in Ouro Preto, with his designs and carving
  • the sanctuary of Bom Jesus de Matosinhos at Congonhas, with twelve soapstone prophets on the front steps and life-size wooden figures of the Passion of Christ in small chapels

In middle age a disease, perhaps leprosy, deformed his hands and feet and left him in pain. Stories say he worked with tools strapped to his arms. Little about his life is certain, and his first biography appeared decades after his death. He became a national hero, seen as a mixed-race genius of a truly Brazilian art.
